title: The Empty Wall: How a Theft Made the Mona Lisa Famous
facts: Stolen Monday 21 August 1911 while the Louvre was closed; thief wore a white worker's smock
Glass case and frame removed on a service staircase; panel hidden under the smock
Painter Louis Béroud found four iron pegs on 22 August 1911
Louvre closed for a week; crowds (including Franz Kafka) came to see the empty space
Apollinaire arrested in September 1911; Picasso questioned; both cleared
Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian ex-Louvre worker who helped build the protective case; police accepted his alibi
Kept the painting about two years (28 months to arrest) in a trunk
Wrote to Florence dealer Alfredo Geri; Uffizi director Giovanni Poggi authenticated it; arrested December 1913
Patriotic motive (return it to Italy); sentence 1 year 15 days, served about seven months
Returned to the Louvre in January 1914; before the theft it was not the most visited work in the museum
Panel 77 x 53 cm, oil on poplar
notes: Newspaper mastheads and headlines on screen are illustrative, not reproductions of real 1911 front pages. Portraits are stylised drawings, not likenesses.
